mcqs.question: Which redesign options address lock contention on a hot path, according to the answer skeleton?
options: Only ever increasing the number of CPU cores available to the process
Rewriting the entire service in a different programming language
Switching every lock to a ReentrantLock with fairness enabled, regardless of the workload
Sharding the lock into independent stripes, replacing it with a lock-free structure, or moving non-essential work out of the critical section
mcqs.explanation: These three are the concrete, nameable redesign techniques the skeleton calls for. Adding cores doesn't fix contention on a single shared lock, a language rewrite is an enormous non-answer, and switching to a fair ReentrantLock by default doesn't address the underlying contention shape.

mcqs.question: In the StripedCounter example, why do two threads incrementing keys that hash to different stripes never contend with each other?
options: Each stripe has its own independent lock object, so threads on different stripes acquire different locks and never wait on each other
Because Java automatically parallelizes array writes at different indices
Because increment() is annotated with a special no-contention keyword
Because the JVM guarantees array accesses never require synchronization
mcqs.explanation: Sharding works specifically because each stripe is protected by its own lock object, so two threads on different stripes are never waiting on the same monitor. Java doesn't auto-parallelize array writes, there's no such keyword, and array accesses to shared mutable state generally do need synchronization.

mcqs.question: If the actual bottleneck is a slow network call happening while a lock is held, what fixes it?
options: Switching the lock to a fairness-enabled ReentrantLock
Moving the network call outside the critical section, holding the lock only for the brief in-memory update
Replacing the lock with a lock-free CAS loop around the same network call
Increasing the number of stripes in a sharded lock design
mcqs.explanation: None of sharding, lock-free structures, or fairness settings fix a critical section that's slow because of I/O — the lock isn't the problem, the work inside it is. Moving the network call out of the locked region is the only fix that addresses the actual bottleneck.

mcqs.question: Why is jumping straight to a lock-free CAS-loop redesign, without checking simpler fixes first, usually the wrong first move?
options: Lock-free CAS loops are always slower than a synchronized block, in every case
The Java compiler rejects CAS loops unless a lock has already been proven insufficient
Lock-free code is harder to write correctly, and sharding or shrinking the critical section often removes most of the contention with far less risk
CAS loops require a special hardware feature most production CPUs don't support
mcqs.explanation: Lock-free code carries real correctness risk and complexity that sharding or a smaller critical section usually avoids while capturing most of the throughput gain. CAS isn't always slower, the compiler enforces no such ordering rule, and CAS is a standard feature on essentially all modern production CPUs.
